paras: The attempted lynching of Dock Bacon and Anderson Finch took place at Chase City, Mecklenburg County, Virginia, early on July 24, 1903, when armed white men gathered to take summary action against two Black prisoners accused of attempting to assault a white woman. The crowd desisted, and both men were convicted within a week and legally hanged, Finch on September 2 and Bacon on October 3, after Finch recanted his testimony against Bacon. The Richmond Planet called Bacon's execution "a judicial murder."

According to a Chase City dispatch, on the night of July 22 a man threw meal in the face of a married white woman, later named as Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan, seized her on her portico, and fled when her screams drew help. A posse arrested four Black men the next morning, Dock Bacon, Anderson Finch, Monroe Stokes and John Dunlop, and a crowd surrounded the guarded jail.

About 1 a.m. on July 24, after word spread that a prisoner had confessed, armed white men met near the Banner Warehouse. The Times-Dispatch correspondent present wrote that some said the chance of acquittal "demanded immediate and summary action," but that "wise counsel prevailed." The guards gave a different account: a party of seventy-five to a hundred men broke open the Chase City prison and took the men out before handing them back to the officers.

Finch said Bacon made the attack while he kept watch; Bacon denied it. Twelve men with Winchester rifles took the two to the county jail at Boydton, and Stokes and Dunlop were to be released for lack of evidence. When Chase City people appeared in Boydton and every horse and buggy in Chase City was reported hired, the sheriff moved the prisoners by train; a lynching party had reportedly formed "for the avowed purpose of executing the men." Returned July 25, they were indicted and sent to Petersburg for safe-keeping.

At the July 28 trial, held under military guard, Bacon had no counsel until the judge asked a lawyer to act, and the jury convicted him in about twenty minutes. Finch was convicted as an accessory, and Judge Holmes sentenced both to hang on September 2.

On August 3 Finch told a reporter he had lied about Bacon because at his arrest "they put a rope around my neck and threatened to hang me." A Petersburg jail officer said he believed Bacon innocent, and Petersburg residents, white and Black, raised a fund for a new trial. At the request of Commonwealth's Attorney E. C. Goode, Governor Montague respited Bacon, while Finch was hanged on September 2.

A second respite came minutes before Bacon's scheduled hanging on September 4; his spiritual adviser, the Rev. Ferrell, wrote that an angry crowd gathered and Bacon was slipped out to a train. Bacon was hanged at Boydton on October 3, declaring on the scaffold that he was innocent, before a crowd including many Chase City people. The governor said doubts of guilt were unsupported by facts; no arrests of the July crowd appear in the coverage.

The Richmond Times-Dispatch covered the case throughout, under headlines such as "Lynching Averted" and "Dock Bacon Will Hang." Its July reports gave the crowd's case without comment. Short items ran elsewhere, such as the New-York Tribune's "Must Hang for Attempted Rape."
Later the Times-Dispatch defended the respite as a guard against "a judicial murder," while the Staunton Spectator remarked that Mecklenburg "has at last had the pleasure of hanging Doc Bacon."

No Black-press report of the July crowd or the trial was found; the Richmond Planet took up the case in October with Ferrell's letters and a report headlined "An Innocent Man Executed." Its editorial called Finch's testimony "extorted," asked whether the judge would have hanged a white man, and said Bacon died "to appease the blood-thirsty taste of a howling mob."

The seizure rests on the guards' account and a Fredericksburg rewrite; the correspondent at the meeting reported only that the crowd was talked out of acting. Finch's statements shifted from accusing Bacon at trial and sentencing to recanting in August, though one report said he admitted his own guilt. By the Planet's account he declared Bacon innocent on the gallows.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Dock Bacon and Anderson Finch
bases: An armed crowd of white men gathered at night to take summary action against two Black prisoners accused of an attempted assault on a white woman and, by the guards' account, took them out of the Chase City prison before being persuaded to give them back (A3, A4, A7); a second lynching party was reported formed the next night (A6).

The crowd of armed white men, numbered at 75-100 by the guards, acted without authority on a crime accusation but killed no one (A3, A4). Finch (Sept. 2) and Bacon (Oct. 3) died by legal execution after indictment, trial and sentence (A9, A16, A24), which the Richmond Planet called 'a judicial murder' (A27, A29) but which does not meet the definition.

Separate Chase City and Boydton correspondents of the Times-Dispatch (A3, A4, A6) and the Fredericksburg Free Lance (A7) agree that an armed crowd gathered to lynch the prisoners and was persuaded to desist; they differ on whether the men were actually taken from custody.

accounts.gist: Armed white men met near the Banner Warehouse about 1 a.m. after word of a confession; some urged summary action, but 'wise counsel prevailed' and a lynching was prevented.

accounts.gist: A lynching party of seventy-five to a hundred men broke open the Chase City prison and took the men out, then was persuaded to return them to the officers.

accounts.label: Boydton correspondent, July 25
accounts.gist: A lynching party formed at Chase City the next night to execute the men, but the sheriff had them moved by train first.

accounts.label: Anderson Finch
accounts.gist: First said Bacon made the attack while he watched; after conviction told a reporter he had lied because a rope was put around his neck at his arrest.

accounts.label: Boydton correspondent's review of the trial
accounts.gist: Meal found on Bacon's hat and in his hair the next morning, and a failed alibi, corroborated Finch's testimony.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Rev. Ferrell)
accounts.gist: Goode told him he believed Bacon not guilty and wired for a thirty-day respite; an angry crowd at Boydton forced the sheriff to arm extra deputies and spirit Bacon away.

accounts.label: Governor Montague
accounts.gist: Doubts about Bacon's guilt were not sustained by facts that would warrant setting aside the verdict, so he did not intervene further.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'Lynching Averted' and reported the crowd's case for 'summary action' without comment while calling the assailant 'the flend' and 'the brute.'
The Times-Dispatch editorial defended the respite, saying Bacon should be allowed to show 'if he can' that he was innocent.
The New-York Tribune ran a telegraph brief headlined 'Must Hang for Attempted Rape.'
The Staunton Spectator mocked Mecklenburg for having 'at last had the pleasure of hanging Doc Bacon.'
The Richmond Planet headlined 'An Innocent Man Executed' and editorially called the hanging a 'judicial murder' to appease 'a howling mob.'

info: Armed crowd met about 1 a.m. on July 24, 1903 (night of July 23-24); the alleged assault was about 11 p.m. Wednesday, July 22; a second lynching party was reported formed at Chase City on the night of July 24.
Chase City, Virginia; crowd met near the Banner Warehouse; the guards said the Chase City prison was broken open.
Dock (Doc) Bacon and Anderson Finch, Black prisoners ('negroes'); Monroe Stokes and John Dunlop were also arrested on suspicion and were to be released for lack of evidence.

Attempted criminal assault on Mrs. C. E. Geoghegan, a white married woman, on her portico at night; meal thrown in her face and she was seized by the throat. Finch was accused as an accessory who kept watch.
A crowd of armed white men of Chase City ('citizens of Chase City'); none named.
None by the crowd. Finch was legally hanged September 2 and Bacon October 3, 1903, at Boydton.

Finch hanged at Boydton September 2; Bacon respited twice (to September 4, then thirty days) and hanged at Boydton October 3, protesting his innocence; body sent to the medical department of the University of Virginia.
